## Overview and purpose

`unitroottools` provides unit-root and stationarity tests for the **Applied Time Series Econometrics (ATSE)** course at **Universidad Carlos III de Madrid**, with one consistent interface and full transparency about how each decision was reached. It is the R companion of the Python package [UnitRoot-Tools](https://github.com/maarranz/UnitRoot-Tools); both follow a common, language-neutral [specification](https://github.com/maarranz/UnitRoot-Tools-R/blob/main/spec/specification.qmd).

This document describes the software/API. The ATSE course material provides the econometric theory; the Labs provide worked examples and exercises. A longer tutorial is the package vignette, [rendered here](vignette.html).

Three conventions hold throughout:

- **Every result says how it was obtained**: hypotheses in words, deterministic terms, number of lags and how they were chosen, effective sample, critical values *and their source*, p-value, decision.
- **Decisions are taken from critical values** computed for the actual sample size; the p-value is computed for the same sample size and agrees with them.
- **Nothing is dropped silently.** Missing values, irregular dates or several candidate columns are errors that say what to fix.

### What R already provides

| unitroottools | Closest existing R tool | Why the function is kept |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `adf()` | `urca::ur.df()`, `tseries::adf.test()` | MAIC/MBIC lag selection on a common sample, MacKinnon critical values *and* p-values at the effective sample size, the φ statistics with their tables, full selection table |
| `ur_strategy()` | — | Dolado–Jenkinson–Sosvilla-Rivero / Enders procedure, a conservative variant and Hamilton's rule, each step recorded |
| `pp()` | `urca::ur.pp()` | Follows the published formula (urca's version differs by up to 0.1 in small samples); p-value |
| `dfgls()` | `urca::ur.ers()` | Lag selection by Perron and Qu (2007); finite-sample critical values and p-value (urca's are too liberal: about 8% size at a nominal 5% with T = 100) |
| `kpss()` | `urca::ur.kpss()`, `tseries::kpss.test()` | Same statistic; kernels and automatic bandwidths; critical values and p-value from the exact limiting distribution (the published table is off in the third decimal) |
| `tidy()`, `glance()` | — | Results of any test as data frames |

## Installation and loading

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("maarranz/UnitRoot-Tools-R", build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

Dependencies (`urca`, `generics`) are installed automatically. Building the vignette needs [pandoc](https://pandoc.org), which comes with RStudio; without it, leave out `build_vignettes = TRUE` and read the vignette [here](vignette.html). To install a specific version, add the tag: `"maarranz/UnitRoot-Tools-R@v0.2.0"`.

```r
library(unitroottools)
```

### Example used below

The logarithm of U.S. real GDP, 1947Q1–2012Q4 (264 observations), the example Enders uses for the testing of unit roots when the deterministic terms are unknown. The data come with the package.

```r
gdp  <- read.csv(system.file("fixtures", "enders_rgdp.csv", package = "unitroottools"))
lgdp <- ts(log(gdp$rgdp), start = c(1947, 1), frequency = 4)
```

## The augmented Dickey–Fuller test

The test regression is

$$
\Delta y_t = a + \gamma t + b\, y_{t-1} + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \beta_j \Delta y_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t ,
\qquad H_0: b = 0 \ \text{(unit root)} \quad H_1: b < 0,
$$

with `trend = "n"` (no deterministic terms), `"c"` (constant, $\gamma = 0$) or `"ct"` (constant and trend).

```r
adf(lgdp, trend = "ct")
```

```
Augmented Dickey-Fuller test (tau3)

  H0: unit root
  H1: stationary around a linear trend
  Deterministics: constant and linear trend
  Lags: 1 (MAIC, kmax = 15)
  Effective sample: N = 262 (t = 3, ..., 264)

  Statistic:        -1.489
  Critical values:  1%: -3.994   5%: -3.427   10%: -3.137
  Source:           MacKinnon (2010) response surface
  p-value:          0.831

  Decision at 5%: do not reject H0 (unit root)
```

`summary()` adds the φ statistics (joint tests of the unit root and the deterministic terms) with their critical values, the lag-selection table and the test regression. Arguments: `lags` (fixed number of lagged differences), `max_lags`, `criterion` (`"MAIC"`, `"MBIC"`, `"AIC"`, `"BIC"`), `final_sample`, `level` (0.01, 0.05 or 0.10) and `var` (column of a data frame).

### Choosing the number of lags

`select_lags()` compares $k = 0, \dots, k_{\max}$, with $k_{\max} = \lfloor 12 (T/100)^{1/4} \rfloor$ (Schwert 1989), **on the same observations**, and returns the whole table. The default criterion is the modified AIC of Ng and Perron (2001), computed on the series detrended by OLS. After selection, `adf()` re-estimates the test regression with all observations available for the chosen order; `final_sample = "common"` keeps the selection sample.

```r
select_lags(lgdp, trend = "ct")    # MAIC selects k = 1 out of 0, ..., 15
```

## Which deterministic terms? Specification strategies

`ur_strategy()` decides the deterministic terms and tests for a unit root in one call, recording every step:

- `"original"`: the Dolado–Jenkinson–Sosvilla-Rivero sequence as set out by Enders: $\tau_3$, $\phi_3$, a test of the trend given the unit root, a conditional test; then the same with a constant only; finally $\tau_1$.
- `"conservative"`: as the original, but a non-rejection by $\tau_2$ keeps the constant and stops.
- `"hamilton"`: you declare whether the series is trending (`trending = TRUE` or `FALSE`, no default); one test follows.

```r
ur_strategy(lgdp, "original", lags = 1)
```

```
Specification strategy: Original (Dolado-Jenkinson-Sosvilla-Rivero / Enders)

  Lags: 1 (fixed)
  Sample (all regressions): N = 262 (t = 3, ..., 264)   Level: 5%

  Step Regr.  Test       Statistic Crit.val.  p-value  Decision    Next
  1    ct     tau3          -1.489    -3.427    0.831  not reject  test phi3
  2    ct     phi3           2.966     6.337    0.471  not reject  go to stage C
  3    c      tau2          -2.049    -2.873    0.266  not reject  test phi1
  4    c      phi1          25.485     4.631  < 0.001  reject      test constant, b = 0 imposed
  5    aux_c  t(const)       6.797     1.969  < 0.001  reject      conditional t test of b
  6    c      t(b) cond.    -2.049    -1.651    0.021  reject      stop

  Specification: constant
  Conclusion:    no unit root: stationary around a non-zero mean

  Note: p-values are for each step on its own;
  no p-value or size is reported for the sequence as a whole.
```

The original procedure removes the trend and then rejects the unit root through a conventional t test justified by the constant, a conclusion Enders himself rejects for GDP. The conservative variant keeps the constant and does not reject (`unit root (constant retained)`); Hamilton's rule with `trending = TRUE` uses $\tau_3$ only (`unit root (with drift)`). The history (`$history`, or `tidy()`) separates rejections of the unit root from rejections that only decide the path of the procedure.

## Other tests

```r
pp(lgdp, trend = "ct")       # Phillips-Perron Z_tau
dfgls(lgdp, trend = "ct")    # Elliott-Rothenberg-Stock DF-GLS
kpss(lgdp, trend = "ct")     # KPSS: H0 is stationarity
ng_perron(lgdp, trend = "ct")  # Ng-Perron M tests (MZ_t reported; MZ_a, MSB, MP_T alongside)
ers_pt(lgdp, trend = "ct")     # ERS point-optimal P_T
boot_ur(lgdp, trend = "ct", B = 999, seed = 1)   # bootstrap ADF (needs bootUR)
```

- **`pp()`** corrects the Dickey–Fuller t ratio for serial correlation with a kernel estimate of the long-run variance (Phillips and Perron 1988; Hamilton 1994, eq. 17.6.8). Critical values and p-value as for $\tau$; the normalized-bias statistic $Z_\alpha$ is reported alongside, with its own critical values and p-value.
- **`dfgls()`** detrends by GLS ($\bar c = -7$ or $-13.5$). Without `lags`, the number of lags is chosen as Perron and Qu (2007) recommend: MAIC on the OLS-detrended series. Critical values and p-value come from the package's own finite-sample simulation over the sample size and the number of lags (out-of-sample size at 5%: 4.8–5.3%).
- **`ng_perron()`** and **`ers_pt()`** use the same GLS detrending and lag choice as `dfgls()`, with the autoregressive estimate of the spectral density at frequency zero (Ng and Perron 2001; Elliott, Rothenberg and Stock 1996). `statistic =` chooses which M statistic is the test (`"MZt"` by default); the others are reported alongside. All reject for small values. Critical values and p-values come from the package's own simulation, tabulated over $T$ and $k$ and interpolated in $1/T$ (out-of-sample size at 5%: 4.0–5.8%). With few observations and several lags they can be far from the asymptotic values, because the spectral estimate is unstable (at $T = 25$ with 6 lags the 5% critical value of $MZ_\alpha$ is about −800), and the result then warns that the test can hardly reject; with a trend, the limits differ slightly from Ng and Perron's Table 1 (see D15 in the specification).
- **`boot_ur()`** runs the bootstrap ADF test or the union-of-rejections test of the bootUR package (Smeekes and Wilms), install it with `install.packages("bootUR")`. Six bootstrap schemes (`bootstrap = "AWB"` by default, `"BWB"`, `"DWB"`, `"MBB"`, `"SB"`, `"SWB"`), `union = TRUE` for the union test, `B` replications and a `seed`. The result has a bootstrap p-value and no critical values; the decision uses the p-value.
- **`kpss()`** reverses the hypotheses: rejection is evidence *against* stationarity. Critical values and p-value from the exact limiting distribution (eigenvalues of the Brownian-bridge covariance kernel and Imhof's formula).
- **Long-run variance** (`pp()` and `kpss()`): `kernel = "bartlett"` (default), `"parzen"` or `"qs"`; `bandwidth = "short"` (default) or `"long"` (Schwert's rules), a number of autocovariances, `"andrews"` (Andrews 1991) or `"newey-west"` (Newey and West 1994). For KPSS, Hobijn, Franses and Ooms (2004) recommend `kernel = "qs", bandwidth = "newey-west"`.

## Results as data frames

`glance()` gives one row per test, `tidy()` one row per statistic (on a strategy: one row per outcome, and the history):

```r
tests <- list(adf(lgdp, trend = "ct"), pp(lgdp, trend = "ct"),
              dfgls(lgdp, trend = "ct"), ng_perron(lgdp, trend = "ct"),
              kpss(lgdp, trend = "ct"))
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tests, glance))
res[, c("test", "statistic_name", "statistic", "p_value", "reject", "lags", "nobs")]
```

```
       test statistic_name statistic p_value reject lags nobs
1       ADF           tau3   -1.4891  0.8312  FALSE    1  262
2        PP          Z_tau   -1.1105  0.9243  FALSE    5  263
3    DF-GLS        tau_GLS   -1.0193  0.8625  FALSE    1  262
4 Ng-Perron            MZt   -1.0664  0.8445  FALSE    1  262
5      KPSS        eta_tau    0.7008  0.0000   TRUE    5  264
```

All five point the same way for log GDP: the unit root is not rejected, and stationarity around a trend is rejected.

## Critical values and p-values

| Statistic | Critical values | p-value |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $\tau$ (ADF), $Z_\tau$ (PP) | MacKinnon (2010) response surfaces at the effective $N$; MacKinnon (1996) without deterministic terms | MacKinnon (1996), finite-sample, same $N$ |
| $\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3$ | Own response surfaces in $(T, k)$ from a Monte Carlo simulation (code in `data-raw/`); they reproduce Dickey and Fuller's (1981) tables without lags | MacKinnon's (1996) method on the same surfaces |
| $Z_\alpha$ (PP) | Own response surface for the Dickey–Fuller normalized bias, which has the same limit | same surface |
| DF-GLS | Own response surfaces in $(T, k)$ from a Monte Carlo simulation | MacKinnon's (1996) method on the same surfaces |
| Ng–Perron M tests, ERS $P_T$ | Own simulation, tabulated in $(T, k)$ and interpolated in $1/T$ | MacKinnon's (1996) method on the same quantiles |
| Bootstrap (`boot_ur()`) | none | bootUR's bootstrap p-value |
| KPSS | Exact limiting distribution (kernel eigenvalues, Imhof inversion) | same distribution |
| Conditional and auxiliary t tests in strategies | Student t | Student t |

Every result records its source in `$calibration`, and warns when the sample is below 25 observations or outside the simulated range.

## Compact API summary

| Function | Purpose | Returns |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `adf(y, trend, lags, max_lags, criterion, final_sample, level, var)` | Augmented Dickey–Fuller test | `ur_test` |
| `select_lags(y, trend, max_lags, criterion, var)` | Lag order by MAIC, MBIC, AIC or BIC, with the full table | `ur_lags` |
| `ur_strategy(y, strategy, trending, allow_no_constant, lags, max_lags, criterion, final_sample, level, var)` | Deterministic terms and unit-root decision, step by step | `ur_strategy` |
| `pp(y, trend, kernel, bandwidth, level, var)` | Phillips–Perron $Z_\tau$ (and $Z_\alpha$) | `ur_test` |
| `dfgls(y, trend, lags, max_lags, criterion, level, var)` | DF-GLS test | `ur_test` |
| `kpss(y, trend, kernel, bandwidth, level, var)` | KPSS test of stationarity | `ur_test` |
| `ng_perron(y, trend, lags, max_lags, criterion, statistic, level, var)` | Ng–Perron M tests | `ur_test` |
| `ers_pt(y, trend, lags, max_lags, criterion, level, var)` | ERS point-optimal test | `ur_test` |
| `boot_ur(y, trend, bootstrap, B, union, detrend, lags, max_lags, criterion, criterion_scale, seed, level, var)` | Bootstrap ADF or union test through bootUR | `ur_test` |
| `simulate_df(T, R, trend, seed)` | Simulated Dickey–Fuller distribution, with `plot()` | `df_simulation` |
| `tidy(x)`, `glance(x)` | Results as data frames | data frame |
| `match_trend(trend)` | Canonical deterministic code from an alias | string |
| `new_ur_test()`, `validate_ur_test()` | Build and check a result object (for developers) | `ur_test` |

A `ur_test` is a list: `statistic`, `statistic_name`, `critical_values`, `p_value`, `reject`, `level`, `tail`, `trend`, `lags`, `lag_selection`, `nobs`, `sample`, `calibration`, `other_statistics` (e.g. the φ statistics), `engine`, `warnings`, `regression`, `call`. Accepted inputs: numeric vectors, `ts`, `zoo`, `xts`, data frames, tibbles and tsibbles (choose a column with `var`).

### Agreement with the Python version

Both implementations follow the same [specification](https://github.com/maarranz/UnitRoot-Tools-R/blob/main/spec/specification.qmd), which records every convention as a numbered decision. The ADF regressions, φ statistics and auxiliary tests are checked against 120-digit reference calculations shared with the Python package (agreement better than $3 \times 10^{-15}$), and the $\tau$ critical values agree to $10^{-15}$. Known differences of the Python version are listed in [notes-for-python.md](https://github.com/maarranz/UnitRoot-Tools-R/blob/main/spec/notes-for-python.md).

### Rebuilding the HTML

The examples are ordinary R code blocks, validated in a fresh session rather than executed during rendering. Equations are rendered as MathML, which needs no external script or fonts. With Quarto (or pandoc) installed, from the repository root:

```bash
quarto pandoc docs/unitroottools_Documentation.qmd \
  --from markdown --to html5 --standalone --toc --toc-depth=2 \
  --mathml --embed-resources -o docs/index.html
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("vignettes/unitroottools.Rmd",
  output_format = rmarkdown::html_vignette(math_method = "mathml"),
  output_dir = "docs", output_file = "vignette.html")'
```
